themes.title: Selene & The Moon

facts.text: Selene, the Greek Titaness of the Moon, drove her silver chariot across the night sky, illuminating the world with borrowed light — a reminder that even reflection can be a form of brilliance.
The Moon controls the tides of the ocean and the tides of the mind. In Vedic thought, Chandra governs the Manas — the emotional mind — and its phases mirror the cycles of human desire and detachment.

Selene fell in love with the mortal Endymion, asking Zeus to grant him eternal sleep so he would never fade. The Moon's love is possessive — it wants to freeze beauty in time, yet beauty exists only because it passes.

The Moon has no light of its own. It shines only by reflecting the Sun. In the same way, the ego believes it is the source of its achievements, forgetting that all capability is borrowed from forces greater than itself.
The night sky has always been a canvas for human projection. We see faces, animals, and gods in the stars — not because they are there, but because the mind seeks meaning in chaos.
In many cultures, the new moon is considered a time for planting seeds — both literal and metaphorical. Darkness is not emptiness; it is the womb from which light is born.
The Moon's gravitational pull creates the tides, but it also subtly affects the water within our bodies. We are, in a very real sense, lunar beings — creatures of the tide.

The Moon is slowly drifting away from Earth at 3.8 cm per year. In a billion years, total solar eclipses will be impossible — the Moon will appear too small to cover the Sun. Even celestial relationships have expiration dates.

Ptolemy believed the Moon's influence caused tides, madness, and the cycles of life. While science has explained the tides, the Moon still governs the menstrual cycle, the migration of birds, and the spawning of coral — life itself dances to the Moon's rhythm.

quotes: The Moon is a friend for the lonesome to talk to. — Carl Sandburg
We are all like the bright moon, we still have our darker side. — Kahlil Gibran
The Moon, like a flower in heaven's high bower, with silent delight sits and smiles on the night. — William Blake
Do not swear by the moon, for she changes constantly, so your love would also change. — Shakespeare
The Moon is the first milestone on the road to the stars. — Arthur C. Clarke

themes.title: Ego & Arrogance

facts.text: The Bhagavad Gita warns: 'The ego is the greatest enemy of the human soul.' When Arjuna asks Krishna about the nature of the self, the answer is not 'I am great' but 'I am not the doer.'
Arrogance is the ego's armor. But armor is heavy — it slows the warrior. The Gita teaches that true strength comes not from the assertion of self but from the surrender to dharma.
In the ocean of existence, arrogance is a wave that believes it is separate from the sea. It rises, it crashes, and it returns — never having been anything but water.

The Shiv Purana describes ego (ahamkara) as the first veil that separates the individual soul from Shiva — pure consciousness. To remove the ego is not to destroy the self but to discover its infinite nature.
True art requires the death of the ego. The painter who paints for fame paints nothing true. The musician who plays for applause hears nothing real. Creation begins where the self ends.
The ego thrives on comparison. It measures itself against others and finds either superiority or inadequacy — both are illusions. The self needs no comparison to exist.
When Krishna tells Arjuna 'You have the right to work, but never to the fruit of work,' he is describing the end of ego-driven action. Act, but let go of the need to be the hero of your own story.

Nietzsche warned that 'whoever fights monsters should see to it that in the process he does not become a monster.' The ego, in its quest to prove its strength, often becomes the very thing it opposes.

The Dunning-Kruger effect reveals that the least competent are often the most confident, while the truly skilled doubt themselves. Arrogance is not a sign of ability — it is a sign of ignorance about the depth of one's own ignorance.

quotes: The ego is not master in its own house. — Sigmund Freud
In the fields of observation, chance favors only the prepared mind. — Louis Pasteur
The more I learn, the more I realize how much I don't know. — Albert Einstein
The greatest enemy of knowledge is not ignorance, it is the illusion of knowledge. — Daniel Boorstin
Pride is a kind of wolf that lives in a man's heart and never dies. — African Proverb

themes.title: Bhagavad Gita

facts.text: The Bhagavad Gita begins not with wisdom but with despair. Arjuna, the greatest warrior, drops his bow and says, 'I will not fight.' The scripture teaches that the darkest moment precedes the greatest clarity.
Krishna's central teaching: 'You have the right to work, but never to the fruit of work.' This is not passivity — it is the ultimate freedom. Act fully, attach to nothing.

The Gita describes the soul as 'unborn, eternal, ever-existing, undying, and primeval.' It is not slain when the body is slain. This is not metaphor — it is the foundational axiom of Hindu philosophy.

In Chapter 11, Krishna reveals his Vishvarupa — the Universal Form — containing all worlds, all beings, all time. Arjuna sees the entirety of existence in one being and trembles. The infinite is not abstract; it is terrifyingly real.
The Gita was spoken on a battlefield, not in a temple. Wisdom does not require perfect conditions. The most profound truths are often revealed in the midst of chaos, not in the silence of retreat.

Krishna describes three paths to liberation: Karma Yoga (selfless action), Jnana Yoga (knowledge), and Bhakti Yoga (devotion). The Gita does not prescribe one path — it honors all three as valid ways to the divine.
'Whenever dharma declines and the purpose of life is forgotten, I manifest myself.' The Gita teaches that the divine does not abandon the world — it returns, again and again, to restore balance.

The Gita's 700 verses were spoken in approximately 90 minutes — the time between Arjuna's collapse and his decision to fight. The most transformative wisdom in human history was delivered in a single, urgent conversation on the edge of war.

Einstein kept a copy of the Bhagavad Gita on his bedside table. When asked if he believed in God, he said he believed in 'the God of Spinoza who reveals himself in the orderly harmony of what exists' — a sentiment that echoes the Gita's vision of cosmic order.

quotes: You are what you believe in. You become that which you believe you can become. — Bhagavad Gita
The soul is neither born, and nor does it die. — Bhagavad Gita 2.20
When meditation is mastered, the mind is unwavering like the flame of a lamp in a windless place. — Bhagavad Gita 6.19
The self-controlled soul, who moves amongst sense objects, free from either attachment or repulsion, he wins eternal peace. — Bhagavad Gita 2.64
You have the right to work, but never to the fruit of work. You should never engage in action for the sake of reward, nor should you long for inaction. — Bhagavad Gita 2.47

themes.title: Shiv Purana

facts.text: In the Shiv Purana, Shiva is described as Nirguna — without attributes, without form, without beginning or end. He is not a god among gods but the ground of being itself, the silence between notes.
The Shiv Purana teaches that the universe is Shiva's dance — the Tandava. Every atom moves in rhythm. Destruction is not the opposite of creation; it is its partner in an eternal dance.

Shiva drank the poison Halahala to save the universe, turning his throat blue. The Neelakantha — the blue-throated one — teaches that the willingness to suffer for others is the highest form of divinity.

The Shiv Purana describes the damaru — Shiva's drum — as the source of all language and music. The first sound, Nada, is the vibration from which all creation emerges. Music is not entertainment; it is cosmology.

Shiva sits in meditation on Mount Kailash, the axis mundi, the center of the world. His stillness is not inactivity — it is the stillness of a mind that has transcended all duality, all desire, all fear.
In the Shiv Purana, Parvati asks Shiva: 'What is the essence of all the Vedas?' He replies: 'The sound Om. It is the syllable from which all of creation chants itself into existence.'
Shiva is called Mahakala — the great time. He is not bound by time; he is time itself. Past, present, and future are all one in the dance of Mahakala.

Shiva is called Tryambaka — the three-eyed one. The third eye represents the eye of wisdom that sees beyond the duality of good and evil, self and other, creation and destruction. When it opens, the universe is consumed in flame — not as punishment, but as liberation.

The Nataraja statue of Shiva dancing within a ring of fire is one of the most recognized symbols in the world. Physicist Fritjof Capra wrote that 'the dance of Shiva is the dance of subatomic matter' — modern physics and ancient mythology converging on the same truth.

quotes: I am the death that carries off all things, and the source of things to come. — Shiva, Bhagavad Gita 10.34
The root of joy is in the mind, and the root of the mind is in the Self. — Shiv Purana
He who sees the Supreme Lord dwelling equally in all beings, undestroyed in the destroying, truly sees. — Inspired by Shiv Purana
Silence is the language of the divine. All else is a poor translation. — Inspired by Shiv Purana
In the embrace of the divine, the dancer and the dance become one. — Inspired by Shiv Purana

themes.title: Art & Beauty

facts.text: Art is not what you see, but what you make others see. The painter does not copy the world — they translate it, filtering reality through the lens of emotion, memory, and dream.
The sunflower turns its face to the light. In this simple act is a metaphor for the spiritual life — the constant orientation of the soul toward what illuminates, even when the source is hidden.
A star field is a reminder of scale. Every point of light is a sun, perhaps with planets, perhaps with life. The universe is not indifferent — it is generous beyond comprehension.

The flute is the oldest instrument — a hollow reed that sings when breath passes through it. It teaches that music is not made but revealed, not created but discovered in the space between silence and sound.
Waves are the ocean's way of communicating with the shore. Each one is unique, yet all are the same water. Identity is like a wave — real in its moment, eternal in its substance.
Beauty is not in the object but in the eye that perceives it. The same sunset can be mundane or miraculous depending on the state of the observer's mind.
The Japanese concept of 'wabi-sabi' finds beauty in imperfection — the cracked pot, the weathered stone, the fading flower. It teaches that transience is not the enemy of beauty but its essence.

Van Gogh painted 'The Starry Night' from an asylum window, yet it became the most recognized painting in history. The greatest art often emerges not from comfort but from the depths of human suffering — beauty forged in the furnace of pain.

The golden ratio (1.618) appears in sunflower seed spirals, nautilus shells, and the proportions of the Parthenon. It is as if the universe has a preferred aesthetic — a mathematical beauty that underlies all form.

quotes: Every artist dips his brush in his own soul, and paints his own nature into his pictures. — Henry Ward Beecher
The purpose of art is washing the dust of daily life off our souls. — Pablo Picasso
I dream my painting and I paint my dream. — Attributed to many artists
Art is not what you see, but what you make others see. — Edgar Degas
I found I could say things with color and shapes that I couldn't say any other way — things I had no words for. — Georgia O'Keeffe
